## What are we trying to understand?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson bias-lesson"><p>Suppose a researcher wants to estimate the average attention-test score of all students at a hypothetical college. Morning classes are easy to visit, but evening classes are harder to reach. If the researcher collects many scores from morning students, will the estimate describe the entire college accurately?</p><p>This optional Week 2 lesson uses a small, completely known synthetic population to explore how sampling design affects what researchers can conclude. No real student data are used.</p><div class="clt-overview"><p><strong>Learning goals</strong></p><ol><li>Distinguish a target population, sampling frame, and sample; identify undercoverage.</li><li>Explain why increasing sample size reduces sampling variability but does not necessarily remove bias.</li><li>Compare simple random, convenience, and proportionate stratified sampling.</li><li>Distinguish random sampling from random assignment.</li></ol><p><strong>Before starting:</strong> Review populations, samples, quantitative variables, and the idea of an average. The spread of repeated sample means is introduced visually here and developed formally in Week 6.</p></div></div>
~~~

## Make a prediction and explore

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson bias-lesson" id="bias-lesson"><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="prediction"><legend>If we sample more morning students but never include evening students, will the coverage problem disappear?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-prediction" value="yes"> Yes. A sufficiently large sample is always representative.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-prediction" value="no"> No. The same group is still excluded.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-prediction" value="unknown"> Only if the sample mean is exactly 50.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check prediction</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><section class="clt-simulator" aria-labelledby="bias-explore"><h2 id="bias-explore">Compare two ways of selecting students</h2><div class="bias-population"><h3>Our target population: 500 students</h3><p>Every student belongs to one of two groups. Maximum 20,000 samples per method.</p><h3>Who was included in the most recent sample?</h3><div class="bias-sample-grid"><div class="bias-sample"><h4>A · Simple random sample</h4><div class="bias-composition" aria-hidden="true"><span class="bias-morning" data-bar="a-morning"></span><span class="bias-evening" data-bar="a-evening"></span></div><p data-output="a-composition">No sample drawn yet.</p><p>Sample mean: <strong data-output="a-latest">—</strong></p></div><div class="bias-sample"><h4>B · <span data-output="comparison"></span></h4><div class="bias-composition" aria-hidden="true"><span class="bias-morning" data-bar="b-morning"></span><span class="bias-evening" data-bar="b-evening"></span></div><p data-output="b-composition">No sample drawn yet.</p><p>Sample mean: <strong data-output="b-latest">—</strong></p></div></div><div class="bias-legend"><span><i class="bias-key bias-morning" aria-hidden="true"></i>Morning students</span><span><i class="bias-key bias-evening" aria-hidden="true"></i>Evening students</span></div><h3>What happens across many samples?</h3><p>Each sample contributes one average to its histogram. Look for both the location and the spread of the accumulating estimates. <strong data-output="count">0</strong> samples per method.</p><div class="bias-chart-wrap" data-chart="means"></div><div class="bias-legend"><span><i class="bias-key truth" aria-hidden="true"></i>True population mean = 50</span><span><i class="bias-key average" aria-hidden="true"></i>Average of simulated estimates (solid line)</span></div><p class="clt-caption">Both plots use the same horizontal scale, one-point intervals, and frequency scale. Their vertical scale adjusts together as samples accumulate. Each histogram represents repeated sample means, not individual students.</p><table class="bias-table"><caption>Compare estimates across all simulated samples</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Statistic</th><th scope="col">A · Random</th><th scope="col">B · Comparison</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Average estimate</th><td data-output="a-mean">—</td><td data-output="b-mean">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Observed bias (average − 50)</th><td data-output="a-bias">—</td><td data-output="b-bias">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Observed SD of estimates</th><td data-output="a-sd">—</td><td data-output="b-sd">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Expected estimate</th><td data-output="expected-a">—</td><td data-output="expected-b">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Theoretical bias</th><td data-output="bias-a">—</td><td data-output="bias-b">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Theoretical SD of estimates</th><td data-output="theoretical-a">—</td><td data-output="theoretical-b">—</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="clt-caption">Observed bias and spread fluctuate in finite runs. The theoretical values describe the repeated-sampling behavior of the specified design. The theoretical standard deviation accounts for sampling without replacement; the formula is not required for this introductory activity.</p></section></div>

## Interpret what you find

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson bias-lesson"><ol><li>Start at n = 10 with morning-only convenience sampling. Draw one sample for each method. Who appears in each sample? Are the two estimates necessarily close to 50?</li><li>Draw 1,000 samples for each. Compare the centers of the histograms and the observed bias. Which method estimates the population mean more accurately on average?</li><li>Change n to 100 and draw another 1,000 each. Compare the spread of estimates with your previous run. Does a narrower histogram guarantee the estimates are centered at 50?</li><li>At the same sample size, switch to proportionate stratified sampling. Draw one sample, then 1,000. Compare the group counts, average estimates, and variability with the simple random sample. What does stratification accomplish in this constructed population?</li></ol><p><strong>Think about it:</strong> In an actual survey, the true population mean is usually unknown. What information about the sampling frame and recruitment process would help you judge whether the results represent the target population?</p></div>
~~~

## What is the sampling design telling us?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson bias-lesson"><p>The <strong>target population</strong> is the full group we want to describe. A <strong>sampling frame</strong> is the set of units accessible for selection. The <strong>sample</strong> is the subset actually observed. In Method B’s convenience scenario, the morning-only frame excludes evening students, producing undercoverage. We draw randomly within the morning frame here to isolate that problem; convenience sampling in practice need not be random even within the accessible group.</p><p>In <strong>simple random sampling without replacement</strong>, every possible sample of a fixed size from the full population is equally likely. A sample need not match the population proportions exactly. Across repeated samples, however, its mean is centered at the population mean. In <strong>proportionate stratified sampling</strong>, we divide the population into groups and select randomly within each group in proportion to its size. Here, both groups are represented by design, and the simple sample mean is an unbiased estimator. Disproportionate stratification may require weighting.</p><div class="bias-formula"><strong>Bias versus sampling variability</strong><br>Bias = expected estimate − true population value<br>Sampling variability = how much estimates vary from sample to sample</div><p><strong>Why this makes sense:</strong> In this population, morning students average 42 and the entire population averages 50. A morning-only sample is centered at 42 regardless of how many morning students we select. Its theoretical bias is −8. Increasing the sample size reduces the spread of repeated estimates, not the eight-point bias. A large sample can therefore be consistently wrong.</p><p>Random sampling and random assignment are different: random sampling concerns how participants are selected from a population, while random assignment concerns how recruited participants are assigned to study conditions. Random assignment helps support causal comparisons when the experimental design and assumptions are appropriate; it does not automatically make the recruited sample representative.</p><p>Other issues, such as nonresponse, self-selection, and measurement bias, can also distort results. This activity isolates one source of bias, undercoverage, rather than simulating every possible research problem.</p></div>
~~~

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson bias-lesson" id="bias-knowledge-check"><p>These four questions revisit the learning goals. Your answers stay in your browser.</p><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="frame"><legend>1. Why does the morning-only sampling frame create undercoverage?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-frame" value="small"> It has too few students to calculate an average.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-frame" value="excluded"> Evening students cannot be selected, even though they belong to the target population.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-frame" value="random"> Randomly selecting from the morning frame makes every college student equally likely to enter the sample.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="size"><legend>2. Increasing the morning-only sample from 10 to 100 can do what?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-size" value="remove"> Eliminate the eight-point theoretical bias.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-size" value="precise"> Reduce variability of estimates without removing the bias.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-size" value="perfect"> Guarantee an estimate of the entire population mean.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="strata"><legend>3. What does proportionate stratified sampling do here?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-strata" value="within"> Draw randomly within morning and evening groups, using their population proportions.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-strata" value="one"> Select everyone from one randomly chosen group.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-strata" value="same"> Guarantee each sample mean equals exactly 50.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="assignment"><legend>4. Which statement correctly distinguishes random sampling and random assignment?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-assignment" value="same"> They are the same procedure.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-assignment" value="different"> Sampling selects participants; assignment allocates recruited participants to study conditions.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="bias-q-assignment" value="cause"> Random sampling alone proves that a treatment causes an outcome.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><p><strong>Takeaway:</strong> A larger sample is not a substitute for a sound sampling design. Consider who can be selected, how they are selected, and what population the results can reasonably describe.</p><p>Textbook connection: OpenStax <em>Introductory Statistics 2e</em>, Chapter 1 (sampling and experimental design). The repeated-sampling comparison anticipates Chapter 7 and the Week 6 lesson.</p></div>
